question: Our relationship managers and compliance officers keep deadlocking over whether to take on high-risk corporate clients, and when the decision is escalated the revenue side usually prevails. How should that escalation body be structured so commercial interests cannot carry the decision?
summary: The corpus supports a governance model in which escalation and higher-risk relationship decisions are structured around the three lines of defence, with the AML/compliance function positioned independently of the revenue-generating business, and with decisions taken (and documented) at senior management level. Basel sets out the three lines and requires the chief AML/CFT officer to have stature, authority and a direct reporting line to senior management or the board; Wolfsberg requires the escalation path to be independent and available to all staff; StAR/EBA place termination-or-continuation and PEP approval decisions with senior management (or a committee including at least one senior manager), with the group AML/CFT compliance officer involved in higher-risk cases; and the FCA/EBA warn that profitability and relationship-manager closeness must not drive risk decisions. I could NOT support the claim that the audit committee or board should be involved in oversight of decisions to terminate or continue higher-risk relationships — that recommendation in the StAR text is directed at a different (narrower) role, so I have dropped it and substituted what the corpus actually says about board/audit-committee involvement.

drafts.question: Our relationship managers and compliance officers keep deadlocking over whether to take on high-risk corporate clients, and when the decision is escalated the revenue side usually prevails. How should that escalation body be structured so commercial interests cannot carry the decision?
drafts.summary: The corpus directly addresses your situation. The World Bank/StAR "Puppet Masters" study describes exactly this deadlock — relationship manager vs. compliance officer disagreement on client risk — and the client acceptance committee (CAC) as the standard escalation mechanism. Its Recommendation 14 sets the governing principle: compliance must be able to make its voice heard at the highest managerial level, and once compliance has voiced a concern, relationship managers must not have the final say. To make that real, the design levers the corpus supports are: (1) put the chief AML/CFT officer (and, for group-wide cases, the group AML/CFT compliance officer) on the body, with the stature and authority for their concerns to command attention from the board, senior management and business lines; (2) set the seniority of the approving manager by reference to the level of risk, not the size of the account; (3) use decision rules that deny the revenue side a majority — the StAR PEP committee model uses unanimity, a fixed quorum that must always include the CEO, and minuted meetings; (4) document approvals and refusals in writing with clear delineation of responsibility and accountability; (5) define in the customer acceptance policy the circumstances in which the firm will not accept or will terminate a relationship, so the committee is applying a pre-agreed boundary rather than negotiating one; and (6) address the incentive problem directly — the FCA treats risk assessments "unduly influenced by the potential profitability" of a relationship as poor practice, expects firms to manage the risk that a relationship manager becomes too close to a customer to take an objective view, and treats reward structures that take account of AML failings as good practice. Finally, internal audit as third line should periodically review the escalation process itself.

claims.text: The deadlock you describe is a recognised pattern: when a relationship manager and a compliance officer cannot agree on the true risk level of a client and whether its business is acceptable, most banks pass the decision up to a higher level of responsibility, such as a client acceptance committee (CAC).

The governing principle is that banks should ensure their organisational structure lets compliance departments make their voice heard at the highest managerial level, and that once compliance has voiced a concern, relationship managers should not have the final say in deciding whether to accept a client; this is framed as a recommendation that financial institutions have sufficiently independent client acceptance practices.

The board and senior management should appoint an appropriately qualified chief AML/CFT officer with overall responsibility for the AML/CFT function, possessing the stature and necessary authority within the bank such that issues raised by this officer receive the necessary attention from the board, senior management and business lines.

The chief AML/CFT officer should have a direct reporting line to senior management or the board, and where the role is separated from the chief risk officer or chief compliance officer, the relationship between those officers and their respective roles must be clearly defined and understood.

Business units (front office, customer-facing activity) are the first line of defence, while the chief AML/CFT officer and the compliance function form the second line — so the escalation body should not be composed such that the first line can determine second-line risk decisions.

In higher-risk cases the group AML/CFT compliance officer should be involved in the approval process, because that officer is often in the best position to say a person should not be accepted regardless of the size of the account, and because the group-level view captures customers refused or terminated elsewhere in the group, preventing branch- or country-shopping.

A concrete committee design used by a bank in the StAR study gives the committee explicit authority to make decisions on measures to be taken and to provide opinions on whether to continue relationships; members include the CEO, the head of compliance of the business area, the records manager and the customer manager, with occasional participants such as the head of the business area depending on the issue.

In that same committee model, decisions are unanimous, the quorum is at least four participants and must always include the CEO, the committee meets at least quarterly or whenever any permanent participant requests a meeting, and minutes of meetings are kept.
A designated committee whose decisions are unanimous is cited as good practice for deciding whether particular customers continue to pose an increased money laundering risk.

The appropriate level of seniority for sign-off should be determined by the level of increased risk associated with the business relationship, and the approving senior manager should have sufficient seniority and oversight to take informed decisions on issues that directly impact the firm's risk profile.

When deciding whether to approve a higher-risk relationship, senior management should base the decision on the level of ML/TF risk the firm would be exposed to if it entered into the relationship and on how well equipped the firm is to manage that risk effectively.

Whatever the approval policy is, it should be set out in writing and decisions should be documented; good practice is that the decision to accept or continue the relationship is documented with clear delineation of responsibility and accountability, and approval or refusal by each senior manager involved is documented in writing.

Escalation arrangements vary in practice: in some banks a group compliance unit holds final approval over a new higher-risk account, while in others the final decision rests with a group business head, and some banks build in escalation to separate committees or units where the client is thought to pose immediately higher risk or reside in a sensitive jurisdiction.
A bank's customer acceptance policy should define the circumstances under which the bank would not accept a new business relationship or would terminate an existing one.

The FCA treats it as poor practice where money laundering risk assessments are unduly influenced by the potential profitability of new or existing relationships, and as good practice where the firm identifies and effectively manages the risk that a relationship manager might become too close to customers to take an objective view of the money laundering risk.

The FCA cites as good practice that reward structures take account of any failings related to AML compliance, and asks firms how senior management are involved in approving relationships with high-risk customers including PEPs.

A clear escalation path for AML and CTF issues should be implemented, available to all staff, and it should be independent; a lack of clear escalation processes may lead to failure to investigate and report potentially suspicious activity.

At each stage of an escalation the decision to refer or continue, and its rationale, needs to be recorded and kept on file, and the independent and objective third line of defence should periodically review the escalation process.

Internal audit, as the third line of defence, independently evaluates risk management and controls and reports to the audit committee of the board or a similar oversight body through periodic evaluations of the effectiveness of compliance with AML/CFT policies and procedures.
Firms should also consider having the audit committee, board or equivalent corporate body involved in the oversight of decisions to terminate or continue higher-risk relationships.
